title: Processes and signals
summary: ps, top, kill and the signals behind it, jobs, & and nohup.

steps.title: Every program is a process
body: A running program is a **process** with a **PID**, a parent (PPID), an owner and state.
USER   PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY  STAT START TIME COMMAND
$ pgrep -a dotnet      # PIDs + command lines matching a name
$ top                  # live view; P sorts by CPU, M by memory, q quits
`htop` is a friendlier `top` (install it). PID 1 (`systemd` on most distros) is the ancestor of everything.

steps.prompt: The server is slow. Which command shows you, **live**, which process is eating the CPU?
steps.explain: `ps` is a snapshot; `top`/`htop` refresh continuously. `df -h` is disk space.

steps.title: Signals
body: `kill` doesn't necessarily kill: it **sends a signal**.
| `SIGTERM` | 15 | "please exit" (the default). Programs can clean up. |
| `SIGKILL` | 9 | the kernel ends it now. Can't be caught: no cleanup, no flushing. |
| `SIGHUP` | 1 | terminal closed; many daemons treat it as "reload config" |
Etiquette: TERM, wait a few seconds, only then KILL.

steps.prompt: Arrange the polite way to stop a stuck process 912.
steps.explain: Ask first (TERM), give it time, check whether it's still there, and only force it if it is.

steps.prompt: Match the signal to when it's sent.

steps.title: Jobs: &, fg, bg, nohup
body: $ ./long-task.sh &        # start in the background, get the prompt back
$ fg %1                   # bring job 1 to the foreground
$ bg %1                   # let it continue in the background
Background jobs still belong to your terminal: **close the SSH session and they get SIGHUP** and usually die.
nohup ./long-task.sh > task.log 2>&1 &     # ignore SIGHUP, log to a file
For anything long-lived use `tmux`/`screen` for interactive work, or a proper **systemd service** (next lesson).

steps.prompt: You started a 2-hour migration with `./migrate.sh &` over SSH, then your Wi-Fi dropped. When you reconnect, it's gone. What would have prevented this?
steps.explain: The dropped session sent SIGHUP to its jobs. nohup ignores it; tmux keeps a session alive on the server you can reattach to.
Job 1 was terminated (bash may report it once), so only job 2 remains. `+` marks the current job.

steps.title: Find and stop real processes
prompt: Five programs are running on this machine in the background. Look at them with `ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,etime,cmd`
1. Write the PIDs of **all** `report-worker` processes into `~/answers/pids.txt`, one per line.
2. Stop `stuck-export` **politely**, so it can save its progress (it writes a line to `~/export.log` when it gets the right signal).
3. `noisy-logger` ignores the polite signal. Make sure it is gone.

checks.name: pids.txt lists every report-worker
checks.fail: `~/answers/pids.txt` should hold exactly the PIDs `pgrep report-worker` prints (and the workers must still run).

checks.name: stuck-export has stopped
checks.cmd: for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do pgrep -x stuck-export >/dev/null || exit 0; sleep 0.5; done; exit 1

checks.name: stuck-export saved its progress
checks.fail: `~/export.log` has no "clean shutdown" line: the process was killed without a chance to clean up. `kill PID` sends SIGTERM, which it handles; `kill -9` does not let it. Press Reset scenario to try again.

checks.name: noisy-logger is gone
checks.cmd: for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do pgrep -x noisy-logger >/dev/null || exit 0; sleep 0.5; done; exit 1
checks.fail: `noisy-logger` is still running. It ignores SIGTERM, so it needs `kill -KILL` (`-9`).

checks.name: the report workers still run
checks.fail: A `report-worker` was stopped too. Only stop the two programs named in the task.

hints: `pgrep -a report-worker` prints PID and command line; `pgrep report-worker > ~/answers/pids.txt` writes just the PIDs.
`kill PID` (or `pkill -x stuck-export`) sends SIGTERM, the polite "please stop". Then `cat ~/export.log`.
After `pkill noisy-logger`, `pgrep noisy-logger` still finds it. `pkill -KILL -x noisy-logger` cannot be ignored.
explain: Always try SIGTERM first: it lets a program flush buffers, finish a transaction and remove its lock files. SIGKILL is
handled by the kernel and the program never sees it, so anything half-written stays half-written. That is also what
`docker stop` and Kubernetes do: SIGTERM, a grace period, then SIGKILL.

steps.title: Mission: the process hunt
prompt: The fans sound like a jet engine. In **The process hunt**, do **Kill it... for good**: find the CPU hog with `ps` or `top`, and stop the thing that keeps restarting it, not just the process.
steps.explain: A process that comes back after `kill` has a parent (or a supervisor) restarting it. `ps -ef --forest` shows the family tree; stop the parent.
